public_rationale: The claim has three parts. First, LLMs lack knowledge, thoughts, feelings and the ability to learn. Second, that is why they will make mistakes. Third, a mistake passed from one chatbot to another might build a flaw into the software or break the process. The contract records no agreed test for 'knowledge' or 'thoughts', so the first part cannot be checked. The second part depends on the first. Evidence that LLMs make mistakes would not on its own show that the cause he gives is correct. The third part says 'might'. It states a possibility, and the contract does not score it. A paper last revised on 2025-10-26 (e1) describes a taxonomy of 14 failure modes in multi-agent LLM systems. The taxonomy was built from an analysis of 150 traces, and 'inter-agent misalignment' is one of its three categories. The paper does not test whether those failures come from the cause the claim gives. So the claim is not scored.
limitations: The packet holds one context item (e1). It classifies failure modes in multi-agent systems but does not show how often they occur in general use.
Nothing in the packet tests whether LLMs have knowledge, thoughts or lasting learning, or links the absence of these to errors.
The packet does not show error rates for LLMs in general.
The 'might' part of the claim is a possibility and is not tested here.

statement.excerpt: They are Language Models interpreting language without any knowledge or thoughts or feelings or ability to learn, and each time they read something they interpret meaning based on their training data, which means they can (and will!) make mistakes, and when they’re, say, talking to another chatbot to tell it what to do next, that little mistake might build a fundamental flaw in the software, or just break the process entirely.
statement.document_title: I Will Never Respect A Website

from_speaker: without any knowledge or thoughts or feelings or ability to learn
interpret meaning based on their training data
which means they can (and will!) make mistakes
when they're, say, talking to another chatbot
that little mistake might build a fundamental flaw in the software, or just break the process entirely
our_interpretation: The claim is causal: because LLMs work only from training data and lack knowledge, thought, feelings and lasting learning, they will make mistakes.
In context, 'ability to learn' means lasting learning from experience, which he contrasts with humans who have 'the capacity for adaptation'. It does not mean in-context adaptation.
Whether LLMs have 'knowledge' or 'thoughts' is a philosophical question with no agreed test. The causal claim depends on it.
'Can (and will!) make mistakes' is not in dispute. Error rates are documented and no lab claims zero errors. That conclusion does not test the premises.
The multi-agent part says a mistake 'might' build a flaw or break the process. That is a hedged possibility, not a firm prediction, so it is not scored.
Taken together, nothing testable here would separate his causal account from rival accounts. So I do not score it.
criteria.support_condition: Not scored. A scoreable version would need agreed tests for 'knowledge' and 'thoughts' and evidence linking their absence to errors.
criteria.contradiction_condition: Not scored. Showing that LLMs never err, or that their errors have no link to how they are trained, would cut against it. No one claims either.

evidence.excerpt: This process identifies 14 unique modes, clustered into 3 categories: (i) system design issues, (ii) inter-agent misalignment, and (iii) task verification.
evidence.explanation: Shows that failures between agents in multi-agent LLM systems are real and common, which fits the scenario he describes. It does not test whether LLMs lack knowledge or thought, which is what his causal claim rests on.
